narrative:
Your predicted probability of leaving is 73%, meaning the model sees roughly a seven-in-ten chance that you will depart. Because a promotion is an investment in someone expected to stay and grow, this high departure risk is why you were denied the promotion.

The strongest signal was your overall work experience of 6–10 years. Employees predicted to stay more often have only 1–5 years of total experience, so your broader experience likely makes you more mobile and marketable. The second signal was that you reported other job opportunities. This is especially important because only about one in four employees predicted to stay had outside opportunities, so having them strongly pushed the prediction toward leaving. The third signal was your 1–5 years with your current employer. Although this tenure range is common among employees predicted to stay, in your profile it combines with broad experience and outside options to raise the likelihood of departure.

The organization should treat this as a retention-risk signal, not a final judgment of your value. Before revisiting promotion, it should discuss your career path, promotion criteria, and what would keep you engaged. You should also clarify what support, recognition, or development would make staying worthwhile.
